newsitem.title: USA: Companies at odds over right to issue domain names.
newsitem.headline: Companies at odds over right to issue domain names.

text.p: Picking out an identity on the Internet, once a simple exercise, could soon become anything but.

In a matter of months, an Internet policy group announced plans to add to the number of generic top-level domain names, the three-letter codes -- .com, .net, .org, .gov and .edu -- that appear at the end of Web and e-mail addresses and other Internet names.

If the plan from the Internet International Ad Hoc Committee (http://www.iahc.org/) materialises, businesses, groups and individuals will be able to choose from seven new domains including ".web," ".firm," and ".store."

At the same time, a group of maverick organisations is testing the authority of Internet policy-setting groups such as the IAHC and the country's major domain-name registry by filing lawsuits against them and creating domain-name registries of their own.

In late March, pgMedia Inc. (http://www.pgmedia.com), a New York alternative registry formerly called PGP Media, sued Network Solutions Inc. (http://www.netsol.com/), of Herndon, Va., to open access to the domain-name registration market. The suit targets Network Solutions because the company has a five-year contract with the National Science Foundation to register top-level domain names that gives it a virtual lock on that market.

Earlier, Image Online Design Inc. (http://www.iodesign.com/), an alternative registry based in California, sued the IAHC and the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (http://www.iana.org/) for allegedly infringing on its right to sell addresses with the ".web" domain-name suffix.

Also, a group calling itself the Enhanced Domain Naming Service Consortium (http://www.edns.net/), or EDNS, has proposed taking authority for registering domain names away from government contractors and replacing them with free-market forces. EDNS advocates creating an unlimited number of registries and top-level domain names.

While they don't see eye to eye on many things, representatives of several opposing parties agree the stakes in the Internet naming business are high and getting higher as more businesses pour onto the Net. As that happens, the number of desirable second-level domain names -- the part of a company's Internet identity that comes before the three-letter code, such as "reuters" in "reuters.com" -- is dwindling.

According to Network Solutions, 18 months ago the total number of registered second-level domain names was 120,000. Today there are more than 1 million. Network Solutions is registering new names at a rate of 3,000 a day, compared with 300 a month in 1993.

About 88 percent of all domain names registered are in the ".com" category, signifying some type of business. Alternative registries would like to expand the type of top-level domains businesses can choose -- ".law" for law firms or ".computer" for computer companies, for example.
Some of these outfits already offer such alternatives. Dot Registries in Pleasanton, Calif., is selling an Alphabet Registry: ".a," ".b" and so on.
"They could be a useful way to organise things, or be useful to a sponsor; .a' could stand for Apple Computer," said Stephen Page, an EDNS member and founder of Dot Registries.
pgMedia, which does business as name.space, offers around 300 mostly business-related domain names, including ".cameras" and ".computers."

"That would allow companies to put trademark names in front of them, such as 'nikon.cameras' or 'ibm.computers' so the end user could make sense" of the names, said Michael Donovan, a pgMedia attorney.

Whatever attractiveness they might have, new registries haven't taken off yet, mainly because the government controls the "root server" computers that direct traffic over the Internet and those machines don't recognise alternative domain names. Changing software coding on the root servers to recognise the new domain names is easy, officials at the maverick registries contend.
Getting Network Solutions and Internet policy groups to recognise the right of other groups to dole out domain names is the hard part, they said.

"We're going through a governance phase, where we decide how to dole out names," agreed Gabriel Battista, Network Solutions chief executive. "We've been relatively silent until the details are worked out. We think it's right for the industry to work it out amongst ourselves because if we don't, we risk the government coming in and doing it for us."

What's worse than waiting a minute for a Web page to materialise? Try waiting a minute then seeing nothing but a cutesy animated ad banner at the top of the page. Other Web pet peeves: blue text on black background, anything that blinks, and wallpaper so busy the words on top of it are illegible. Send your own Web page pet peeves to me at the e-mail address listed below and I'll include examples in an upcoming column.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
